query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A mid‐range vacuum heat treatment (around 500 °C) induces a beneficial microstructural evolution in the as-sprayed FeNiCrCoCu thin coating – namely, the formation of fine nanotwins, a high density of dislocations, and the emergence of a thin, adherent oxide scale (rich in elements like Cr and Cu) – that together increase microhardness and reduce high-temperature wear. In contrast, higher temperature treatments lead to grain coarsening and reduction in hardness, worsening the wear resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-sprayed FeNiCrCoCu coating with relatively coarse grains, minimal dislocation density, and little to no protective oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Apply a vacuum heat treatment at approximately 500 °C to the as-sprayed coating.
generation.conditions: High-temperature wear testing conditions (e.g., tests at temperatures ≥ 400 °C under significant mechanical load, such as simulated abrasive environments or drilling fluids), ensuring that the coating remains a thin protective layer on conventional metal substrates.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of nanotwins, increased dislocation density, and the development of a thin, adherent protective oxide scale (e.g., chromium and copper oxides) on the coating surface.
generation.mechanism: The moderate heat treatment (around 500 °C) promotes a heterogeneous microstructure with grain refinement (via nanotwin formation) and drives controlled oxidation that forms a protective oxide layer. The combination of increased hardness and a self-healing oxide tribo-layer helps resist abrasive, adhesive, and oxidation wear at high temperatures. Conversely, higher treatment temperatures lead to complete recrystallization and grain coarsening, reducing hardness and wear resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Heat-treated coatings will exhibit a significant increase in microhardness and a reduction in wear rate (lower volume loss and friction coefficient) compared to as-sprayed coatings. In contrast, coatings treated at higher temperatures (e.g., 700–900 °C) will show decreased hardness and increased wear due to grain coarsening and less effective oxide scale formation.
generation.baseline: As-sprayed FeNiCrCoCu coating without any post-deposition heat treatment.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies within the temperature regime relevant to high-temperature protective coatings (approximately 400–900 °C) and under high mechanical loads typical of industrial abrasive or drilling environments. It is specific to thin film coatings on conventional metal substrates.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of oxide scale formation and the density of nanotwins in FeNiCrCoCu may differ from similar HEA systems due to the presence of Cu. Detailed quantitative relationships between heat treatment temperature, microstructural evolution, and wear resistance require further characterization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu thin coatings on identical substrates. Subject one set to no post-treatment (as-sprayed baseline) and the other to a vacuum heat treatment at approximately 500 °C. Then, perform wear tests at elevated temperatures (e.g., around 600 °C) under high normal load conditions while exposing the coatings to abrasive media similar to simulated drilling fluid.
measurements: Wear rate (mm3/N·m) using wear track volume measurements
Microstructural analysis (SEM/TEM) to assess grain size, nanotwin formation, and oxide scale presence
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the vacuum heat-treated coatings do not show a significant increase in microhardness, do not develop the expected nanotwin/oxide microstructure, or if their wear rate and friction coefficient are not significantly lower than those of the as-sprayed baseline under high-temperature wear conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this work, (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA were selected as the composition of coating because of its high strength and corrosion resistance in bulk state, while the corresponding properties of coating remain unknown. Therefore, (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating on the Q235 steel substrate was fabricated by using the plasma spray technique, and the microstructure evolution during preparation process, microhardness, and corrosion behavior in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution were investigated. Furthermore, the phase formation and the corrosion behavior of the coatings were specifically analyzed.

The wear rates of the two coatings at room temperature are very close. The wear rate for the CS and HVOF coatings reaches its the lowest point after vacuum heat treatment at 500 °C. The wear rate of the CS-500 °C coating is 0.2152 mm3 m−1 N−1, which is about 4/5 (0.2651 mm3 m−1 N−1) of that of the HVOF-500 °C coating. The CS coating with 500 °C vacuum heat treatment has the best wear resistance due to having the highest microhardness. The wear rates and wear amounts of the two coatings heat-treated at 700 °C and 900 °C decreases due to the decrease in microhardness. The wear mechanisms of the CS and HVOF coatings before and after vacuum heat treatment are adhesive wear, abrasive wear, fatigue wear and oxidation wear.
